About the issue

When Traditions Stop Being Passed On

Many of India's traditional skills are learned from family elders. When fewer young people learn them, the skills can quietly disappear.

A quiet loss of living skills

Weaving, block printing, pottery, folk painting, music and dance are more than hobbies. They are knowledge built up over hundreds of years, kept alive by people who practise them every day.

A tradition does not live in a museum case. It lives in the hands of the people who know how to do it, and in the young people who learn from them.

Where it happens

All over India, whole villages and towns are known for one craft. These places are called craft clusters. Here are three examples.

Map coming soon. A map of craft clusters is planned for a later version. For now, here is a list.

  • Bagru, Rajasthan

    Hand block printing with natural dyes, by the Chhipa community. Learn about Bagru printing

  • Pedana, Andhra Pradesh

    Block-printed Kalamkari cloth made near Machilipatnam. Learn about Kalamkari

  • Dindigul, Tamil Nadu

    Strong, handmade metal locks, a skill the town has been known for over many years.

Who is affected

  • Artisans and their families

    When fewer people buy handmade goods, artisans earn less, and their children may choose other work.

  • Rural communities

    In many villages a craft is a main source of work. When it fades, the whole village feels it.

  • Young people

    You miss the chance to learn skills, stories and ways of thinking from your own culture.

  • All of us

    Every lost tradition makes the world a little less varied and a little less colourful.

Why traditions are fading

  1. 01

    Low, unsteady income

    Many artisan families earn little, and the money is not regular, so children look for other jobs.

  2. 02

    Machine-made goods

    Factory products are faster and cheaper to make, so handmade work is hard to sell at a fair price.

  3. 03

    Little exposure

    Young people rarely see these skills in daily life, at school or online.

  4. 04

    Fewer elders teaching

    Skills pass from elders to children less and less, as families move and lives get busier.

  5. 05

    Long apprenticeships

    Some crafts take years to learn, and UNESCO notes that young people may choose factory or service jobs instead.

  6. 06

    Hard to know where to start

    Even curious young people often don't know where to find a class or workshop. Sanskriti helps with that.

Cause 05 source: UNESCO, Traditional craftsmanship. Causes 01–04 come from the student's Criteria A research.
